body: ## Book One
1. From my grandfather Verus: good character, and freedom from anger.
2. From what I heard and remember of my father: modesty and manliness.

3. From my mother: reverence for the gods, generosity, and holding back not only from doing wrong but even from thinking of it; and also simplicity in the way she lived, far from the habits of the rich.
4. From my great-grandfather: not to have gone to the public schools, but to have had good teachers at home, and to know that on such things one should spend freely.

5. From my tutor: not to become a fan of the Greens or the Blues at the races, nor of the light-shield or heavy-shield men at the games; to put up with hard work and need little; to do things with my own hands, and not to meddle in other people’s business; and to be slow to listen to slander.

6. From Diognetus: not to get excited about trifles; not to believe what wonder-workers and conjurers say about spells and driving out spirits and the like; not to keep fighting quails or be carried away by such things; to put up with plain speaking; to become at home in philosophy, and to hear first Bacchius, then Tandasis and Marcianus; to write dialogues as a boy; and to want the plank bed and the skin and whatever else belongs to the Greek training.

7. From Rusticus: the realisation that my character needed correcting and looking after; not to be led off into the ambitions of the sophists, nor to write treatises on theory, nor to give little sermons, nor to show off as the man who trains hard or does good deeds for display; to keep away from rhetoric and poetry and clever talk; not to walk about the house in formal dress, or do things of that kind; to write letters simply, like the one he himself wrote to my mother from Sinuessa.

To be easy to call back and easy to make peace with, as soon as those who have been angry with me or wronged me are willing to come back; to read carefully, and not be content with a rough idea of the whole, nor agree quickly with people who talk a lot; and to have come across the notes of Epictetus’s lectures, which he lent me from his own house.

8. From Apollonius: freedom, and a steadiness that takes no chances; to look to nothing else, not even for a moment, but reason; to be always the same, in sharp pain, in the loss of a child, in long illness; and to see clearly, in a living example, that the same man can be most intense and yet relaxed.

Not to be impatient when explaining things; to have seen a man who plainly thought his experience and his skill at teaching principles the least of his good qualities; and to have learned how to accept what seem to be favours from friends, without being made smaller by them, and without letting them pass unnoticed.

9. From Sextus: kindness; the example of a household run like a father’s; the idea of living in agreement with nature; dignity without pretence; looking after the interests of friends with care; patience with ordinary people and with those who form opinions without thinking.

The knack of getting on with everyone, so that his company was more pleasant than any flattery, and at the same time he was held in the greatest respect by the very people he was with; a way of finding and ordering, by a clear method, the principles needed for life.
Never to show any sign of anger or any other passion, but to be at once wholly free of passion and full of affection; to praise without fuss, and to know a great deal without showing it.

10. From Alexander the grammarian: not to find fault; not to pounce scornfully on people who use a foreign word or a bad construction or an odd-sounding phrase, but neatly to bring in the very expression that should have been used, by way of answer, or agreement, or joining in a discussion of the thing itself and not the word, or by some other graceful reminder of that kind.
11. From Fronto: to notice what envy, double-dealing and hypocrisy go with a tyrant’s power, and that on the whole the people we call patricians are somehow rather short on affection.

12. From Alexander the Platonist: not to say often, or without need, to anyone, or to write in a letter, “I am too busy”; and not to keep excusing myself in this way from the duties we owe to the people we live with, on the plea of urgent business.

13. From Catulus: not to brush aside a friend’s complaint, even if it happens to be unreasonable, but to try to put things back as they were; to speak warmly of one’s teachers, as is remembered of Domitius and Athenodotus; and to love one’s children truly.

14. From my brother Severus: love of family, love of truth, love of justice; through him to have come to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, Brutus; to have formed the idea of a state with the same laws for all, run on equal rights and equal freedom of speech, and of a kingship that honours above all the freedom of those it rules.

From him also: a steady and constant regard for philosophy; doing good, giving generously, being hopeful, and trusting that one is loved by one’s friends; being open with those he found fault with; and that his friends never had to guess what he wanted or did not want: it was plain.

15. From Maximus: self-mastery, and not being swept about by anything; cheerfulness in every circumstance, and in illness too; a character well balanced, gentle and dignified; doing what had to be done without complaint.

That everyone believed that he meant what he said, and that whatever he did he did with no bad intent. Never surprised, never startled, never hurried or hesitant, never at a loss, never downcast, never forcing a smile, and never again angry or suspicious.

Doing good, being ready to forgive, being truthful; giving the impression of a man who had never been bent rather than one who had been straightened; that no one ever thought himself looked down on by him, nor would have dared to think himself better than he; and being pleasantly witty.

16. From my father: gentleness, and holding unshakably to decisions reached after careful thought; no vanity about what are thought to be honours; love of work and persistence; listening to anyone with something to offer for the common good; giving each person what he deserved, without fail; knowing from experience when to press and when to let go.

Putting an end to the affairs with boys; his sense of the common good; letting his friends off from always dining with him or always travelling with him, and being found just the same by those who had stayed behind on some business; careful and patient inquiry in council, never giving up the search early, content with first impressions; keeping his friends, never tiring of them and never infatuated; self-sufficient in everything, and cheerful.

Looking far ahead, and arranging the smallest things in advance without fuss; checking the cheering and all flattery directed at himself; always guarding what the empire needed, keeping careful accounts of public spending, and putting up with the blame for it; neither superstitious about the gods nor, with men, a crowd-pleaser or flatterer or seeker of popularity, but sober in everything and steady, never vulgar and never chasing novelty.

Using the comforts of life, which fortune gave him in plenty, without arrogance and without apology, so that he enjoyed them when they were there, simply, and did not miss them when they were not; that no one would have called him a sophist, or a smart talker, or a pedant, but a mature man, complete, above flattery, able to manage his own affairs and other people’s.

Besides this, honouring those who truly practise philosophy, without reproaching the others, nor yet being easily led by them; easy to be with, and gracious without overdoing it; looking after his own body in moderation, not as one in love with living, nor for vanity, nor yet neglecting it, but so that, by his own care, he hardly ever needed a doctor or medicines or ointments.

Above all, giving way without envy to those who had some special ability, in speaking, or in the history of laws or customs or other matters, and helping them eagerly so that each might win credit for his own gifts; doing everything according to the customs of our fathers, without making a show even of this, of keeping the customs.

Not restless or easily shifted, but staying with the same places and the same things; after his attacks of headache, at once fresh and vigorous for his usual work; having few secrets, very few and very rare, and those only about public affairs; prudent and measured in putting on shows, in public building, in handouts and the like, as a man who looks to what needs to be done, and not to the credit for doing it.

He did not bathe at odd hours; he did not love building; he did not fuss about food, or the weave and colour of his clothes, or the good looks of his slaves. His clothes came up from his country house at Lorium; most of his time at Lanuvium; the way he treated the tax-collector at Tusculum who apologised to him; and all his manner was like this.

Nothing harsh in him, nothing shameless, nothing violent, nothing that would make anyone say “he’s sweating over it”; but everything thought out in turn, as if at leisure, calmly, in order, firmly, consistently. What is remembered of Socrates would fit him: that he could both abstain from and enjoy the things that most people are too weak to abstain from and too self-indulgent in enjoying.
To be strong, to endure, and to stay sober in both is the mark of a man with a complete and unbeatable soul, as Maximus showed in his illness.

17. From the gods: to have had good grandparents, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people around me, kinsmen, friends, nearly all of them; and that I never slipped into offending any of them, though I had the kind of disposition that, given the chance, might have led me to do something of the sort; it was the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances arose that would have shown me up.
That I was not brought up any longer than I was with my grandfather’s mistress; that I kept my youth innocent, and did not become a man before my time, but even put it off.

That I was placed under a ruler and father who was to take all my vanity away from me, and to bring me to understand that it is possible to live in a palace without needing bodyguards, or embroidered robes, or torches, or statues of this sort, and the like pomp; but that one can bring oneself very close to the life of a private citizen, without for that being any meaner or slacker in the duties a ruler must do for the common good.

That I had a brother whose character could rouse me to take care of myself, and who at the same time delighted me with his respect and affection; that my children were not born dull or deformed in body; that I did not make more progress in rhetoric and poetry and the other studies, in which I might have been held fast if I had found myself getting on well.
That I was quick to give my tutors the positions they seemed to want, and did not put it off, hoping, since they were still young, to do it later. That I knew Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus.

That I had clear and frequent pictures of what life in agreement with nature is like, so that, as far as the gods and the gifts and help and inspiration that come from them are concerned, nothing prevents me from living according to nature now; and if I still fall short of it, that is my own fault, and comes from not keeping to the reminders, almost the lessons, of the gods.

That my body has held out so long in such a life; that I never touched Benedicta or Theodotus, and that later, when I was caught up in love, I was cured; that, though I was often angry with Rusticus, I never did anything I would have regretted; that my mother, who was to die young, still spent her last years with me.

That whenever I wanted to help someone poor or in any other need, I was never told that I had no money to do it with; and that I myself never fell into such need as to take from another; that my wife is the woman she is, so obedient, so loving, so simple; that I found suitable teachers for my children.

That remedies were given me in dreams, among them against spitting blood and dizziness, as at Caieta; and that, when I set my heart on philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, or sit down to writing books, or analysing syllogisms, or busying myself with the heavens. For all these things need “the help of the gods and of fortune”.
Written among the Quadi, on the river Gran.
## Book Two

1. Say to yourself at dawn: today I shall meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, insolent, treacherous, envious, unsociable. They are all like this because they do not know what is good and what is bad. But I have seen the nature of the good, that it is beautiful, and of the bad, that it is ugly, and the nature of the wrongdoer himself, that he is my kin: not of the same blood or seed, but sharing in the same mind and the same portion of the divine. So I cannot be harmed by any of them, for no one can drag me into what is ugly; and I cannot be angry with my kinsman or hate him. For we were born to work together, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of upper and lower teeth. To work against one another, then, is against nature; and to be angry with someone and turn your back on him is working against him.

2. Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh, a little breath, and the ruling mind. Throw away your books; stop being distracted; it is not allowed. But, as if you were already dying, despise the flesh: blood and bones and a woven net of nerves, veins and arteries. Look too at the breath, what kind of thing it is: wind, and never the same, but every moment breathed out and sucked in again. The third, then, is the ruling mind. Think of it like this: you are old; do not let it be a slave any longer, do not let it be jerked about like a puppet by selfish impulses any longer, and do not let it go on grumbling at what is given you now, or dreading what is to come.

3. The works of the gods are full of providence. The works of fortune are not apart from nature, or from the weaving and interlacing of the things that providence governs. Everything flows from there. And there is also necessity, and what benefits the whole world, of which you are a part. For every part of nature, that is good which the nature of the whole brings, and which preserves it. And the world is preserved by changes, of the elements and of the things made from them alike. Let this be enough for you; let these be your principles. But throw away your thirst for books, so that you do not die grumbling, but truly at peace, and grateful to the gods from your heart.

4. Remember how long you have been putting this off, and how many times the gods have given you extra days and you have not used them. You must now at last understand what world you are a part of, and what governor of the world you have flowed from; and that a limit of time is set for you, and if you do not use it to clear the clouds from your mind, it will go, and you will go, and it will never come again.

5. Every hour, set your mind firmly, as a Roman and a man, on doing what is in front of you with precise and unaffected dignity, with affection, with freedom and with justice; and give yourself rest from all other thoughts. And you will give yourself rest if you do every act of your life as if it were your last, free of all carelessness, of every passionate turning away from the command of reason, of pretence, of self-love, and of discontent with what has been given you. You see how few things a person needs to master in order to live a life that flows well and is like the life of the gods; for the gods will ask nothing more of the one who keeps to these.

6. Go on, insult yourself, insult yourself, my soul; but you will not have the chance to honour yourself much longer. Each person has only one life, and yours is nearly over, and you do not respect yourself, but place your happiness in the souls of other people.

7. Are things that happen to you from outside distracting you? Then give yourself the time to learn something good, and stop wandering round in circles. But you must also beware of the other kind of wandering. For those people are also fools who have worn themselves out with activity in life, and have no target at which to aim every impulse and, in a word, every thought.
8. A person is seldom seen to be unhappy because he does not notice what is going on in someone else’s soul. But those who do not follow the movements of their own soul are bound to be unhappy.

9. Always keep these things in mind: what the nature of the whole is, and what my nature is, and how the one is related to the other; what kind of part it is of what kind of whole; and that no one can prevent you from always doing and saying what is in agreement with the nature of which you are a part.

10. Theophrastus, comparing wrongdoings as one might in a general way, says, like a true philosopher, that wrongs done from desire are worse than wrongs done from anger. For the angry man seems to turn away from reason with a certain pain and an inner tightening; but the man who does wrong from desire, overcome by pleasure, seems somehow more self-indulgent and softer in his wrongdoing. Rightly, then, and worthily of philosophy, he said that a wrong done with pleasure deserves more blame than one done with pain. And on the whole, the angry man is more like someone who has been wronged first and driven to anger by pain; while the other has set out to do wrong of his own accord, carried along by desire to do something.

11. Do everything, say everything, think everything, as one who may leave life at any moment. To depart from among men, if the gods exist, is nothing to fear; for they would not bring you into evil. And if they do not exist, or do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a world empty of gods, or empty of providence?

But they do exist, and they do care about human affairs; and they have put it wholly in a man’s power not to fall into what is truly evil. And if there were anything evil in the rest, they would have seen to that too, so that it would be wholly in a man’s power not to fall into it. But how could something that does not make a man worse make a man’s life worse?

The nature of the whole would not have overlooked this, either through ignorance, or knowing but unable to guard against it or put it right; nor would it have made so great a mistake, through lack of power or lack of skill, as to let good things and bad things happen equally and at random to good people and bad.
But death and life, fame and obscurity, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty, all these happen equally to good people and to bad, being neither fine nor shameful. So they are neither good nor bad.

12. How quickly everything vanishes: in the world, the bodies themselves; in time, the memory of them. What all the things of the senses are like, especially those that tempt us with pleasure, or frighten us with pain, or are trumpeted by vanity; how cheap they are, how contemptible, dirty, perishable and dead: this is for the power of the mind to consider. What are these people, whose opinions and voices give a good name? What is dying? And if one looks at it by itself, and with the analysis of thought takes apart the images attached to it, one will no longer think it anything other than a work of nature; and if anyone is afraid of a work of nature, he is a child. And yet it is not only a work of nature, but one that is good for nature. How a man touches God, and with what part of himself, and in what condition that part of him is when it does.

13. Nothing is more wretched than the man who goes round and round everything, and “searches the things beneath the earth”, as the poet says, and tries to guess what is in the souls of his neighbours, and does not see that it is enough to be with the divine spirit within himself alone, and to serve it truly. And the service of it is to keep it pure of passion, of carelessness, and of discontent with what comes from gods and men. For what comes from the gods deserves reverence for their goodness; and what comes from men deserves affection, because they are our kin; and sometimes, in a way, pity, because they do not know good from bad: a blindness no less than the one that takes away the power to tell white from black.

14. Even if you were going to live three thousand years, or thirty thousand, remember all the same that no one loses any other life than the one he is living, nor lives any other than the one he loses. So the longest and the shortest come to the same. For the present is equal for everyone, and so what is lost is equal too; and so what is lost turns out to be just a moment. For no one can lose either the past or the future: how could anyone take from him what he does not have?

So you must remember these two things. First, that all things from eternity are of the same kind and come round again in circles, and it makes no difference whether you see the same things for a hundred years, or two hundred, or for endless time. Second, that the one who lives longest and the one who will die soonest lose the same. For it is only the present that one can be deprived of, since that is all one has; and no one loses what he does not have.
15. That everything is judgement. What was said to Monimus the Cynic is clear; and clear too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes the good of it, as far as it is true.

16. The human soul insults itself, first and most, when it becomes, as far as it can, an abscess, a kind of growth on the world. For to be angry at anything that happens is to break away from nature, which holds within it the natures of all other things. Next, when it turns away from a person, or even moves against him meaning to harm him, as the souls of angry people do. Third, it insults itself when it is overcome by pleasure or pain. Fourth, when it pretends, and does or says anything falsely and untruly. Fifth, when it lets any action or impulse of its own go at no target, but acts at random and without attention, when even the smallest things ought to be done with reference to the end. And the end of rational creatures is to follow the reason and the law of the most ancient city and commonwealth.

17. Of human life, the time is a point; the substance flowing; the perception dim; the whole body’s make-up quick to rot; the soul a whirl; fortune hard to read; fame without judgement. In a word: all that belongs to the body is a river, all that belongs to the soul a dream and smoke; life is a war and a stay in a foreign land; and fame after death is forgetting.

What, then, can guide us through? One thing, and one only: philosophy. And that means keeping the spirit within us unharmed and undamaged, above pleasures and pains, doing nothing at random, nothing falsely or with pretence, not needing anyone else to do or not do anything; and also accepting what happens and what is given as coming from there, wherever it is, from where it came itself; and above all waiting for death with a cheerful mind, as nothing but the setting free of the elements of which every living thing is made. And if there is nothing terrible for the elements themselves in each one constantly changing into another, why should anyone look askance at the change and dissolution of them all? It is according to nature; and nothing according to nature is bad.
Written at Carnuntum.
## Book Three

1. We should not only reckon that each day our life is being used up and a smaller part of it is left, but also this: that if a man lives longer, it is not at all certain that his mind will still be equal to understanding things, and to the study that leads to knowledge of things divine and human. For if he begins to lose his wits, breathing and eating and imagining and wanting, and all the rest of that kind, will not fail him; but the power to make use of himself, to fill in exactly the measures of his duty, to sort out what appears to him, to judge whether it is now time to take his leave of life, and everything else that needs a well-trained reason, goes out first. So we must hurry, not only because we come nearer to death every day, but also because our grasp of things and our power to follow them may come to an end before we do.

2. We should also notice things like this: that even what happens as a side-effect of nature’s work has its own charm and attraction. When bread is baked, for example, some parts of it split open; and these cracks, which in a way go against the baker’s intention, are somehow becoming, and in their own way make us want to eat.

Figs, again, burst open when they are ripest; and in olives ready to fall, the very nearness to rotting adds a beauty of its own to the fruit. And ears of corn bending down, and the lion’s wrinkled brow, and the foam dripping from a wild boar’s mouth, and many other things, if you looked at them by themselves, are far from beautiful; but because they follow from nature’s work, they add to its beauty and give delight.

So that a man who has feeling and a deeper understanding of what happens in the whole will find that almost nothing, even among the things that come as consequences, fails to fit in with a kind of pleasure. Such a man will look at the real gaping jaws of wild beasts with no less pleasure than at the copies that painters and sculptors show us; he will be able to see a kind of ripeness and bloom in an old woman or an old man, and the loveliness of children, with his own clear eyes; and many such things will strike him, which would not convince everyone, but only the man who has become truly at home with nature and her works.

3. Hippocrates cured many diseases, and then fell ill himself and died. The Chaldean astrologers foretold the deaths of many, and then fate caught up with them too. Alexander, Pompey and Julius Caesar, after so often wiping whole cities off the map and cutting down many tens of thousands of horse and foot in battle, also departed from life one day. Heraclitus, after all his theories about the world ending in fire, died with his insides full of water, smeared with cow dung. Lice killed Democritus, and another kind of vermin killed Socrates. What does this mean? You went on board, you made the voyage, you have come into harbour: get out. If it is into another life, there is nothing empty of gods there either. If into nothing at all, you will stop putting up with pains and pleasures, and stop being a slave to a vessel so much worse than what serves it: for the one is mind and divine spirit, and the other earth and gore.

4. Do not waste what is left of your life in thinking about other people, when it is not for some common good. For you lose the chance of some other work: that is, when you think about what so-and-so is doing, and why, and what he is saying, and what he is thinking, and what he is plotting, and all the things that make you wander away from watching over your own ruling mind.

You must, then, keep out of the chain of your thoughts everything random and pointless, and above all everything nosy and malicious; and you must get used to thinking only the kind of thoughts that, if someone suddenly asked you, “What are you thinking about now?”, you could answer at once and frankly, “This, and this”; so that it would be clear straight away that everything in you is simple and kind, and belongs to a creature made for living with others, one that does not care for pleasures or indulgent fancies at all, nor for rivalry, envy, suspicion or anything else you would blush to admit you had in mind.

For such a man, who no longer puts off being among the best, is a kind of priest and servant of the gods, making use of the god who is set up within him, which keeps the man unstained by pleasures, unwounded by any pain, untouched by any insult, unfeeling towards any wickedness; a fighter in the greatest of fights, not to be thrown by any passion; dyed deep with justice; welcoming with his whole soul everything that happens and is given to him; and not often, and not without great need and for the common good, thinking about what someone else is saying or doing or thinking. For he works only at what is his own, and keeps always in mind what is woven for him out of the whole; and the one he makes good, and the other he is sure is good. For the fate given to each person is carried along with him and carries him along.

He remembers too that everything rational is akin, and that to care for all people is in keeping with human nature; but that one should not hold on to the opinion of everyone, but only of those who live in agreement with nature. As for those who do not live so, he keeps always in mind what kind of people they are, at home and away from home, by night and by day, and what kind of people they mix with. So he takes no account even of praise from such people, who are not even pleased with themselves.

5. Do nothing unwillingly, nor selfishly, nor without examining it, nor pulled in two directions. Do not dress up your thoughts in fine words. Do not talk too much, or busy yourself with too much. Let the god within you be the guardian of a living being who is manly, mature, a citizen, a Roman, a ruler, who has taken up his post like a man waiting for the signal to leave life, ready to go, needing no oath and no man as a witness. And let there be in you cheerfulness, and no need of help from outside, and no need of the peace that others give. You must stand upright, not be held upright.

6. If you find anything in human life better than justice, truth, self-control, courage, and, in a word, than your mind being content with itself, where it makes you act according to right reason, and content with fate in what is given you without your choice; if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul, and enjoy the best thing you have found.

But if nothing appears better than the very spirit set up within you, which has brought its own impulses under its control, which examines its thoughts, which, as Socrates used to say, has drawn itself away from the feelings of the senses, which has placed itself under the gods and cares for human beings; if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else, for once you lean towards it and turn aside, you will no longer be able, without distraction, to put first that good which is your own.

For it is not right that anything of a different kind should stand against the good of reason and of citizenship: such as the praise of the many, or power, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures. All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit in, suddenly take over and carry you away. But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better, and hold on to it. “But the better is what is useful.” If it is useful to you as a rational being, keep to it; but if it is useful to you as an animal, say so, and keep your judgement without conceit; only make sure that you examine it safely.

7. Never value as useful to yourself anything that will force you one day to break your word, to give up your self-respect, to hate anyone, to suspect, to curse, to pretend, to desire anything that needs walls and curtains. For the man who has chosen first his own mind and spirit and the worship of its goodness makes no tragic scene, does not groan, will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Above all, he will live neither chasing after anything nor running away; and whether his soul is to be held in his body for a longer or a shorter time does not concern him in the least. For even if he had to depart right now, he will go as readily as he would set about any other task that can be done with decency and order; taking care through his whole life of this one thing only, that his mind is never turned in a direction that does not belong to a thinking and social being.

8. In the mind of a man who has been disciplined and thoroughly cleansed you will find nothing festering, nothing foul, no hidden sore. Fate does not catch his life unfinished, as one might say of an actor who leaves the stage before finishing and playing out the play. And there is nothing in him servile, nothing affected, nothing clinging, nothing cut off, nothing answerable to others, nothing hiding.

9. Respect your power of forming judgements. Everything depends on it, so that no judgement may ever arise in your ruling mind that is out of keeping with nature and with the make-up of a rational being. And this promises freedom from hasty judgement, friendship with human beings, and following the gods.

10. So throw away everything else and hold on to these few things only; and remember also that each of us lives only this present moment, this instant. All the rest is either already lived, or unknown. Small, then, is the life each one lives; small the corner of the earth where he lives; and small too is the longest fame after death, and even that passed on through a line of little men who will very soon die, and who do not know even themselves, let alone someone who died long ago.

11. To the rules already given, add one more: always make a definition or sketch of whatever presents itself to you, so as to see what kind of thing it is in its own substance, stripped bare, as a whole and in all its parts; and to tell yourself its proper name, and the names of the things from which it was put together and into which it will be broken up.

For nothing is so able to make the mind great as to be able to examine methodically and truly each thing that comes before you in life, and always to look at things in such a way as to consider at the same time what kind of world this is, what use this thing has in it, what value it has for the whole, and what for a human being, who is a citizen of the highest city, of which all other cities are like households; what it is, and what it is made of, and how long it is by nature likely to last, this thing that now makes an impression on me, and what virtue I need for dealing with it: gentleness, courage, truthfulness, good faith, simplicity, self-sufficiency, and the rest.

So you must say of each thing: this has come from God; this from the way things are woven together, the threads of fate spun in with each other, from such a meeting and chance; and this from a fellow member of my tribe, my kinsman and companion, who does not know, however, what is in keeping with his nature. But I do know. And so I treat him according to the natural law of fellowship, kindly and justly; while at the same time, in things that are indifferent, I aim at what each is worth.

12. If you do the work in front of you following right reason, seriously, vigorously, kindly, and without any side-business, but keep your own spirit pure and standing, as if you had to give it back at once; if you hold to this, expecting nothing and avoiding nothing, but content with acting now according to nature, and with heroic truth in what you say and utter, you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.

13. Just as doctors always keep their instruments and knives ready for sudden cases, so you keep your principles ready for understanding things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest, as one who remembers how the two are bound together. For you will not do anything human well without referring it to the divine, nor the other way round.

14. Stop wandering about. You are not going to read your little notebooks, nor the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks, nor the extracts from books that you were saving up for your old age. Hurry, then, to the end; throw away empty hopes, and come to your own help, if you care for yourself at all, while you still can.
15. People do not know how many meanings there are in stealing, sowing, buying, being at peace, seeing what must be done; which is not done with the eyes, but with another kind of sight.

16. Body, soul, mind. To the body belong sensations, to the soul impulses, to the mind principles. To receive impressions like a stamp in wax belongs to cattle too. To be jerked about like a puppet by impulses belongs to wild beasts too, and to effeminate men, and to Phalaris and Nero. To have the mind as a guide to what seem to be duties belongs also to those who do not believe in the gods, and those who betray their country, and those who do what they do once they have shut their doors.

If, then, everything else is shared with the kinds of people I have named, what is left that is special to the good man is this: to love and welcome what happens to him and is spun for him by fate; not to soil the spirit set up within his breast, nor trouble it with a crowd of fancies, but to keep it calm, following God in good order, saying nothing contrary to the truth and doing nothing contrary to justice. And if all men refuse to believe that he lives simply, modestly and cheerfully, he is not angry with any of them, nor does he turn aside from the road that leads to the end of life, which he must reach pure, at peace, ready to go, fitted to his fate without being forced.
## Book Four

1. When the master within us is in keeping with nature, it stands towards whatever happens in such a way that it always adapts easily to what is possible and what is given. For it loves no fixed material, but moves towards its aims with a reservation, and turns whatever is brought in against it into material for itself, as fire does when it masters what is thrown on it. A small lamp would have been put out by those things; but a bright fire very quickly makes what is heaped on it its own, eats it up, and rises higher because of it.
2. Let no action be done at random, nor otherwise than by the rule that makes the art complete.

3. People look for retreats for themselves, in the country, by the sea, in the mountains; and you too are used to longing for such things most of all. But this is altogether the mark of a very ordinary person, when you can retreat into yourself at any hour you like. For nowhere can a person retreat to a quieter or more untroubled place than into his own soul, especially if he has within him things such that, by looking into them, he is at once completely at ease; and by ease I mean nothing else than good order. So give yourself this retreat constantly, and renew yourself. Let the principles you meet there be short and basic, so that, as soon as you come upon them, they will be enough to wash away all your distress, and to send you back without resentment to the things you return to.

For what will you resent? The badness of people? Recall the conclusion that rational beings were born for one another; that putting up with them is part of justice; that they do wrong against their will; and how many people, after quarrelling, suspecting, hating and fighting to the death, have been laid out and burned to ashes; and stop at last. Or will you resent what is given to you out of the whole? Recall the choice: either providence or atoms; and all the proofs that the world is a kind of city. Or will the things of the body still get hold of you? Consider that the mind does not mix with the breath, whether it moves smoothly or roughly, once it has drawn itself apart and recognised its own power; and remember too everything you have heard about pain and pleasure, and agreed with.

Or will a little fame pull you away? Look at how quickly everything is forgotten, and the abyss of endless time on either side, and the emptiness of applause, and how changeable and undiscerning are the people who seem to speak well of you, and how narrow the space it is confined to. For the whole earth is a point, and how tiny a corner of it is this place where we live! And here, how many will praise you, and what sort of people are they?

So from now on, remember the retreat into this little plot of land that is yourself; and above all do not be pulled about or strain yourself, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. And among the things most ready to hand, which you will look into, let there be these two. First, that things do not touch the soul, but stand outside it, quite still; and our troubles come only from the judgement within. Second, that all these things you see will change in a moment, and will be no more; and keep constantly in mind how many changes you have yourself already seen. The world is change; life is judgement.

4. If mind is common to us all, then so is reason, by which we are rational beings. If so, then the reason that tells us what to do and what not to do is common too. If so, law is common too. If so, we are citizens. If so, we share in some kind of commonwealth. If so, the world is a kind of city. For in what other common commonwealth could one say the whole human race shares? And from there, from this common city, comes our mind itself, and our reason, and our sense of law; or where else? For just as the earthy part of me has been given me from some earth, and the watery from another element, and the breath from some source, and the hot and fiery from its own source (for nothing comes from nothing, just as nothing goes away into nothing), so the mind too has come from somewhere.

5. Death is like birth, a mystery of nature: a coming together of the same elements, and a coming apart into the same. Nothing in it, at all, to be ashamed of; for it is not out of keeping with a thinking creature, nor with the plan of its making.

6. Such things are bound to come from such people, of necessity; and whoever does not want this wants the fig tree not to have its juice. In any case, remember this: in a very short time both you and he will be dead, and soon not even your names will be left.
7. Take away the judgement, and “I have been harmed” is taken away. Take away “I have been harmed”, and the harm is taken away.
8. What does not make a man worse than he was does not make his life worse either, nor harm him, from outside or from within.
9. The nature of what is useful has been bound to do this.

10. That “everything that happens, happens justly”. You will find it so if you watch carefully. I do not mean only in the sense that it follows in order, but that it is just, as if someone were giving each thing what it deserves. So go on watching, as you have begun; and whatever you do, do it with this: with being good, in the proper sense of the word “good”. Keep to this in every action.
11. Do not see things as the man who insults you judges them, or as he wants you to judge them; but see them as they really are.

12. You should always have these two things ready. First, to do only what the reason of the ruling and law-giving art suggests for the good of people. Second, to change your mind, if someone is there to correct you and move you away from some opinion. But the change must always come from being persuaded that something is just, or for the common good, or the like; never because it seemed pleasant or popular.
13. “Do you have reason?” “I do.” “Then why not use it? For if that is doing its work, what more do you want?”
14. You have existed as a part. You will vanish into what made you; or rather, you will be taken back, by change, into its seed-reason.
15. Many grains of incense on the same altar. One drops first, another later; it makes no difference.
16. Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you go back to your principles and to honouring reason.
17. Do not act as if you were going to live ten thousand years. What must be hangs over you. While you live, while you can, become good.

18. How much leisure a man gains who does not look at what his neighbour said or did or thought, but only at what he himself is doing, that it may be just and holy. Do not look about at other people’s dark characters, but run straight along the line, not swerving.

19. The man who is excited about fame after death does not picture to himself that every one of those who remember him will very soon die himself; and then again the one who comes after him, until the whole memory of him goes out, passed along by people who are lit and then put out. But suppose that those who will remember you were immortal, and the memory immortal too: what is that to you? I do not say that it is nothing to the dead man; but what is praise to the living, except perhaps for some practical use? For now you are letting go, out of season, of the gift that nature gives, while clinging to something else.

20. Everything that is beautiful in any way is beautiful in itself, and complete in itself, and praise is no part of it. A thing is made neither worse nor better by being praised. I say this even of the things commonly called beautiful, such as material things and works of art. As for what is truly beautiful, what need has it of anything? No more than law, no more than truth, no more than kindness or modesty. Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or spoiled because it is blamed? Is an emerald made worse than it was if it is not praised? Or gold, ivory, purple, a lyre, a little knife, a flower, a shrub?

21. If souls live on, how has the air made room for them from all eternity? And how does the earth make room for the bodies of those who have been buried for so long? Just as here, after the bodies have lasted a while, their change and decay makes room for other dead bodies, so the souls that move into the air, after lasting a while, change and spread and are kindled, being taken back into the seed-reason of the whole; and in this way they make room for those that come to live there after them. This is the answer one might give, supposing that souls live on.

And we should consider not only the number of bodies buried in this way, but also the number of animals eaten every day by us and by other animals. How great a number is used up and, so to speak, buried in the bodies of those who feed on them; and yet the space receives them, by their being turned into blood, and changed into air or fire.
What is the way to the truth in this? To divide it into the material and the cause.
22. Do not wander off; but in every impulse give what is just, and in every impression keep to what you clearly grasp.

23. Everything that suits you suits me, O world. Nothing is too early or too late for me that is in good time for you. Everything is fruit to me that your seasons bring, O nature. From you are all things, in you are all things, to you are all things. The poet says, “Dear city of Cecrops”; and will you not say, “Dear city of Zeus”?

24. “Do few things,” says Democritus, “if you want to be at peace.” Would it not be better to do what is necessary, and what the reason of a creature born for the city requires, and in the way it requires? For this brings not only the peace that comes from doing things well, but also the peace that comes from doing few things. For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a man takes it away, he will have more leisure and less disturbance. So at every turn one should remind oneself: “Is this one of the unnecessary things?” And we should cut out not only unnecessary actions, but unnecessary thoughts too; for then the unnecessary actions that follow them will not follow.
25. Try how the life of the good man goes for you: the man who is content with what is given him out of the whole, and satisfied with his own just action and kindly disposition.

26. You have seen those things; look at these too. Do not trouble yourself; make yourself simple. Someone does wrong? He does wrong to himself. Something has happened to you? Good: everything that happens was fated for you from the beginning out of the whole, and spun for you. In a word, life is short; you must make the most of the present with good sense and justice. Be sober, but relaxed.

27. Either an ordered world, or a jumble thrown together. But surely an ordered world. Or can there be order in you, and disorder in the whole? And that when all things are so distinct, and yet spread through one another, and feel with one another.
28. A black character, a soft character, a stubborn character; brutish, cattle-like, childish, stupid, false, buffoonish, huckstering, tyrannical.

29. If he is a stranger in the world who does not know what is in it, no less a stranger is he who does not know what happens in it. He is an exile who runs away from the reason of the city; blind, who shuts the eye of the mind; a beggar, who needs another and does not have from himself everything useful for life; an abscess on the world, who stands apart and separates himself from the reason of our common nature by being displeased with what happens (for the same nature that produced you produces this); a splinter broken off from the city, who breaks off his own soul from the soul of rational beings, which is one.

30. One man practises philosophy without a shirt, another without a book. Here is another, half naked: “I have no bread,” he says, “and I stay true to reason.” And I have no food from my studies, and I stay true.

31. Love the little craft you have learned, and rest in it. Go through the rest of your life as one who has handed over everything he has to the gods with his whole soul, and has made himself neither tyrant nor slave to any human being.

32. Think, for example, of the times of Vespasian. You will see all the same things: people marrying, raising children, falling ill, dying, making war, feasting, trading, farming, flattering, being arrogant, suspecting, plotting, praying for others to die, grumbling at their lot, falling in love, hoarding, wanting consulships, wanting kingdoms. Well, that life of theirs is no longer anywhere.

Move on again to the times of Trajan. Again all the same things. That life too is dead. In the same way look at the records of other times and of whole nations, and see how many people, after straining every nerve, fell soon after and were broken up into their elements. And above all, go over in your mind those you yourself have known, chasing after empty things, and neglecting to do what was in keeping with their own nature, and to hold on to it tightly and be content with it. And here you must remember that the attention given to each action has its own value and proportion; for then you will not lose heart, if you do not spend more time than is fitting on smaller things.

33. Words that were common long ago are now obscure; and so the names of those who were once much praised are now, in a way, obscure too: Camillus, Caeso, Volesus, Dentatus; and a little later Scipio and Cato, then Augustus too, then Hadrian and Antoninus. For all things fade quickly and become legend, and quickly too complete oblivion buries them. And I say this of those who shone in some wonderful way; as for the rest, as soon as they have breathed their last, they are “unseen, unheard of”. And what, after all, is everlasting remembrance? Altogether empty. What, then, is it that we should give our effort to? This one thing: a just mind, actions for the common good, speech that never lies, and a disposition that welcomes everything that happens as necessary, as familiar, as flowing from the same kind of beginning and spring.
34. Give yourself up willingly to Clotho, the Fate who spins, and let her weave you into whatever things she wishes.
35. Everything lasts only a day, both the one who remembers and the one remembered.

36. Watch continually how all things come about by change, and get used to thinking that the nature of the whole loves nothing so much as to change the things that are and to make new things like them. For everything that exists is in a way the seed of what will come from it. But you think only of seeds that are dropped into the earth or the womb; and that is very unthinking.

37. You will soon be dead, and you are not yet simple, nor untroubled, nor free from suspecting that you can be harmed from outside, nor kind to everyone, nor do you yet place wisdom only in acting justly.
38. Look into their ruling minds, even those of the wise: what they run from, and what they chase after.

39. Your harm does not lie in someone else’s ruling mind, nor in any change or alteration of what surrounds you. Where, then? Where your power of judging about harms is. So let that not make the judgement, and all is well. Even if what is closest to it, your poor body, is cut, burned, festers or rots, let the part that judges about these things keep quiet: that is, let it judge that nothing is bad or good which can happen equally to a bad man and a good one. For what happens equally to the one who lives against nature and the one who lives according to nature is neither according to nature nor against it.

40. Think constantly of the world as one living being, with one substance and one soul; and how everything goes back into its one awareness; and how it does everything by one impulse; and how all things work together as causes of all that happens; and how they are spun and woven together.
41. You are a little soul carrying a corpse, as Epictetus used to say.
42. There is nothing bad for things in the process of change, as there is nothing good for things that come into being by change.
43. Time is a kind of river of things that happen, and a violent current. As soon as each thing has been seen, it is swept away, and another is being carried past, and that too will be swept away.
44. Everything that happens is as usual and familiar as the rose in spring and fruit in summer; so too are illness and death and slander and plotting, and everything that delights or grieves fools.

45. What comes after always follows naturally on what went before. It is not like a list of separate items that merely follow one another by necessity, but a reasonable connection; and just as the things that exist are arranged together in harmony, so the things that come into being show not a mere succession, but a wonderful kinship.

46. Always remember the saying of Heraclitus, that the death of earth is to become water, and the death of water to become air, and of air to become fire, and the other way round. Remember too the man who forgets where the road leads; and that people are at odds with the very thing they are most constantly in touch with, the reason that governs everything; and that what they meet with every day seems strange to them; and that we must not act and speak as if asleep, for in sleep too we think we act and speak; and that we must not be like children who take things from their parents, that is, simply because that is how we were taught.

47. If one of the gods told you that you would die tomorrow, or at any rate the day after, you would not think it much better to die the day after rather than tomorrow, unless you were utterly mean-spirited; for how big is the difference? So too, do not think it a great thing to die after many years rather than tomorrow.

48. Think constantly how many doctors have died, after frowning so often over their patients; how many astrologers, after foretelling the deaths of others as if it were something great; how many philosophers, after arguing endlessly about death or immortality; how many great warriors, after killing so many; how many tyrants, after using their power over men’s lives with terrible arrogance, as if they were immortal; how many whole cities, if I may put it so, have died: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others.

Go over, too, all the people you know, one after another: one buried another and was then laid out himself, and another buried someone else, and all in a short time. In a word: always see how short-lived and cheap human things are; yesterday a drop of mucus, tomorrow a mummy or ashes. So pass through this tiny moment of time in keeping with nature, and end your journey content, as an olive might fall when it is ripe, praising the earth that bore it and thanking the tree that grew it.
49. Be like the headland, against which the waves break continually; but it stands firm, and the swelling waters around it are put to sleep.

“I am unlucky, because this has happened to me.” No: “I am lucky, because, though this has happened to me, I go on free from distress, neither crushed by the present nor afraid of what is coming.” For this could have happened to anyone; but not everyone would have gone on free from distress. Why, then, is that a misfortune, rather than this a piece of good fortune? Do you call anything at all a misfortune for a man that is not a failure of man’s nature? And do you think it a failure of man’s nature, when it is not against the will of his nature? Well then.

You have learned what that will is. Does what has happened prevent you, then, from being just, high-minded, self-controlled, sensible, careful in judgement, truthful, modest, free, and all the rest, by whose presence man’s nature has what is its own? From now on, whenever something leads you towards distress, remember to use this principle: not “this is a misfortune”, but “to bear it nobly is good fortune”.

50. A plain but effective help towards despising death is to go over in your mind those who clung tightly to life. What did they gain more than those who died young? They all lie somewhere at last: Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus, Lepidus, and any others like them, who carried many out to burial, and then were carried out themselves. Altogether, the interval is small; and through how many troubles, and with what kind of people, and in how feeble a body, it is dragged out! So do not make much of it. Look at the vast gulf of time behind you, and the other infinity in front. In this, what difference is there between a baby that lives three days and a man who lives three generations, like Nestor?

51. Always run by the short road; and the short road is the one according to nature: so as to say and do everything in the soundest way. For such a purpose frees a man from toil and strain, and from all managing and cleverness.
## Book Five

1. At dawn, when you are reluctant to get up, have this thought ready: “I am getting up to do the work of a human being. Why then am I still grumbling, if I am going out to do what I was born for, what I was brought into the world to do? Or was I made for this, to lie under the blankets and keep warm?” “But this is more pleasant.” Were you born, then, for pleasure? In a word, for being acted upon, or for acting? Do you not see the little plants, the sparrows, the ants, the spiders, the bees, all doing their own work, each helping to put the world in order in its own way? And you are unwilling to do the work of a human being? You do not run to do what is in keeping with your own nature?

“But one must rest too.” I agree. But nature has set limits to this too, as it has to eating and drinking; and yet you go beyond the limits, beyond what is enough; but in your actions, not so: there you stay well within what you could do. The truth is, you do not love yourself; for if you did, you would love your nature and what it wants.

People who love their crafts wear themselves out over their work, unwashed and unfed. Do you value your own nature less than the metal-engraver values engraving, or the dancer dancing, or the miser money, or the vain man his bit of fame? These people, when they are keen on something, would rather not eat or sleep than fall behind in what they care about. And do actions for the common good seem to you cheaper, and less worth your effort?
2. How easy it is to push away and wipe out every troublesome or unsuitable impression, and at once to be in perfect calm.

3. Judge yourself worthy of every word and act that is in keeping with nature, and do not let the criticism or talk of some people that follows distract you. If it was right to do or say it, do not think yourself unworthy of it. Those people have their own ruling mind and follow their own impulse. Do not look round at them; go straight ahead, following your own nature and the common nature; and the road of both is one.

4. I go on through the things that are according to nature, until I fall and rest, breathing my last into the air from which I draw breath every day, and falling onto the earth from which my father gathered his seed, my mother her blood, and my nurse her milk; from which for so many years I have been fed and watered every day; which carries me as I walk on it, and lets me use it for so many things.

5. They cannot admire you for quickness of wit. Very well. But there are many other things of which you cannot say, “I have no gift for it.” Show those, then, which are wholly up to you: sincerity, dignity, hard work, indifference to pleasure, not complaining about your lot, needing little, kindness, freedom, simplicity, not chattering, greatness of mind. Do you not see how many things you could show already, where there is no excuse of lack of talent or unfitness, and yet you still choose to stay down below? Or are you forced by lack of talent to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your poor body, to try to please, to show off, to toss about so much in your soul? No, by the gods; you could have been rid of all this long ago, and been accused, if at all, only of being rather slow and dull of understanding. And even this must be trained, not ignored, and not enjoyed as an excuse.

6. One kind of person, when he has done someone a good turn, is quick to put it down to his account as a favour owed. Another is not so quick to do this, but still thinks of the other as in his debt, and knows what he has done. A third kind, in a way, does not even know what he has done, but is like a vine that has borne grapes and asks for nothing more once it has produced its own fruit.

A horse that has run, a dog that has tracked, a bee that has made honey, and a man who has done good: he does not shout about it, but moves on to the next, as a vine moves on to bear its grapes again in season. You should be one of those who do this, in a way, without noticing. “Yes, but one should notice this very thing; for it is the mark of a social being,” he says, “to be aware that he is acting socially, and, by Zeus, to want his fellow to be aware of it too.” What you say is true; but you are misunderstanding what I am saying now, and so you will become one of those I mentioned first; for they too are led astray by a kind of plausible reasoning. But if you are willing to understand what I am saying, do not be afraid that it will make you neglect any act for the common good.
7. A prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, on the ploughed fields of the Athenians and on their plains.” Either we should not pray at all, or we should pray like this, simply and freely.

8. Just as we say, “Asclepius has prescribed this man riding, or cold baths, or walking barefoot,” so we can say, “The nature of the whole has prescribed this man illness, or disability, or loss, or something else of the kind.” In the first case, “prescribed” means something like this: he ordered this for this man as suited to his health. In the second, what happens to each person has been ordered for him, in a way, as suited to his fate.

For we say that things “fit” us, as builders say that the squared stones in walls or pyramids fit, when they fit together into a certain structure. For in all there is one harmony; and just as the world, this great body, is made up of all bodies, so fate, this great cause, is made up of all causes.

Even quite simple people understand what I mean; for they say, “It brought him this.” So this was brought to this man, and this was ordered for this man. Let us accept these things, then, as we accept what Asclepius prescribes. Many of those prescriptions are harsh too; but we welcome them in the hope of health.

Think of the carrying out and completion of what the common nature has decided as being like your own health. And so welcome everything that happens, even if it seems rather hard, because it leads there: to the health of the world, and the well-being and success of Zeus. For he would not have brought this to anyone, if it were not for the good of the whole; for not even an ordinary nature brings anything that does not suit what it governs.

So there are two reasons why you should be content with what happens to you. One, that it happened to you, was ordered for you, and was related to you in some way, spun for you from the beginning out of the most ancient causes. The other, that even what comes to each person individually is a cause of the well-being, the completion, and, by Zeus, the very survival of what governs the whole. For the whole is maimed if you cut off anything at all from its connection and continuity, of its causes as of its parts. And you do cut it off, as far as you can, when you are discontented; and in a way you destroy it.

9. Do not be disgusted, or give up, or lose heart, if you do not always manage to act on right principles; but when you are knocked off course, come back again, and be glad if most of what you do is worthy of a human being; and love what you are returning to. Do not go back to philosophy as to a schoolmaster, but as people with sore eyes go back to the sponge and the egg, or another to a poultice or a hot compress. In this way you will not be making a show of obeying reason, but will rest in it. Remember that philosophy wants only what your nature wants; but you wanted something else, not in keeping with nature. What could be more pleasant than this? Is that not how pleasure trips us up? But look and see whether greatness of mind, freedom, simplicity, good feeling and holiness are not more pleasant. And what is more pleasant than wisdom itself, when you think how sure-footed and smooth-flowing in everything is the power of understanding and knowledge?

10. Things are wrapped in such a veil that not a few philosophers, and not ordinary ones either, have thought them altogether beyond our grasp; and even the Stoics think them hard to grasp. And every judgement we make can change; for where is the man who never changes his mind? Pass on, then, to the objects themselves: how short-lived they are, how cheap, and how they can belong to a pervert or a prostitute or a robber. Then pass on to the characters of the people you live with, of whom it is hard to put up with even the most agreeable, not to say that a man can hardly put up with himself.

In such darkness and dirt, in such a flood of substance and time, of movement and things moved, what there is that deserves to be valued, or to be taken seriously at all, I cannot imagine. On the contrary, one must comfort oneself and wait for one’s natural release, and not be impatient at the delay, but rest in these thoughts alone: first, that nothing will happen to me that is not in keeping with the nature of the whole; and second, that it is in my power never to act against my god and the spirit within me. For no one can force me to go against it.

11. What am I using my soul for now? Ask yourself this at every turn, and examine yourself: what is there now in this part of me that they call the ruling mind? And whose soul do I have now? A child’s? A youth’s? A silly woman’s? A tyrant’s? A beast of burden’s? A wild animal’s?

12. You can learn what kind of things the many think are good from this. If someone has in mind things that are truly good, such as wisdom, self-control, justice, courage, he could not, with these in mind, bear to hear the comic poet’s line, “He has so many good things...”; for it would not fit. But if someone has in mind what the many think are good, he will listen, and readily accept the comic poet’s line as fitting. So even the many have a sense of the difference; otherwise the line would not offend and be rejected in the one case, while in the case of wealth and the lucky breaks that bring luxury or fame we accept it as fitting and witty. Go on, then, and ask whether we should value and think good those things which, when we have them in mind, the line fits, that the man who owns them is so well supplied “he has nowhere left to relieve himself”.

13. I am made of a cause and of matter. Neither of these will perish into nothing, just as neither came into being out of nothing. So every part of me will be assigned, by change, to some part of the world; and that again will change into another part of the world, and so on to infinity. It was by such a change that I came into being, and my parents, and so on back to another infinity. For nothing prevents us from saying this, even if the world is governed in limited cycles.

14. Reason and the art of reasoning are powers that are enough for themselves and for their own work. They start from their own first principle, and travel to the end set before them; and that is why such actions are called “right actions”, meaning the rightness of the road.

15. None of these things should be called a man’s which do not belong to a man as a man. They are not demanded of a man; man’s nature does not promise them; they are not what makes man’s nature complete. So neither is man’s end to be found in them, nor what completes the end, the good. Besides, if any of these things did belong to a man, it would not belong to him to despise them and stand up against them; nor would the man who makes himself independent of them be praised; nor would the man who goes without some of them be good, if they really were goods. But as it is, the more a man strips himself of these things, or of others like them, or puts up with being stripped of them, the better he is.

16. Your mind will be like the things you often think about; for the soul is dyed by its thoughts. Dye it, then, with a constant stream of thoughts like these: where a man can live, there he can also live well; but he can live in a palace; so he can also live well in a palace. And again: each thing is drawn towards what it was made for; and where it is drawn, there is its end; and where its end is, there is its good and its advantage; so the good of a rational being is fellowship. For it was shown long ago that we were born for fellowship. Or was it not clear that the lower things exist for the sake of the higher, and the higher for the sake of one another? And living things are higher than lifeless ones, and rational beings higher than those that merely live.
17. To chase after the impossible is madness; and it is impossible for bad people not to do things of this kind.

18. Nothing happens to anyone that he is not made by nature to bear. The same things happen to another, and either because he does not know they have happened, or because he wants to show his greatness of mind, he stays firm and unharmed. It is a strange thing, then, that ignorance and the wish to please should be stronger than wisdom.

19. Things themselves do not touch the soul at all. They have no way into the soul, and cannot turn it or move it. The soul alone turns and moves itself; and whatever judgements it thinks fit to make, it makes the things that come before it to match them.

20. In one way a human being is the thing nearest to us, in so far as we must do good to people and put up with them. But in so far as some of them stand in the way of my proper work, a human being becomes to me one of the indifferent things, no less than the sun, or the wind, or a wild beast. These may hinder some action of mine; but they are no hindrance to my intention or my disposition, because of the reservation and the power of turning things round. For the mind turns round and converts every obstacle to its action into a means to its aim; and what holds up the work becomes the work, and what stands in the way on the road becomes the road.

21. Honour the most powerful thing in the world: that is, what uses all things and directs all things. And in the same way honour the most powerful thing in yourself: that is, what is akin to it. For in you too it is this that uses everything else, and your life is directed by it.

22. What does not harm the city does not harm the citizen either. Whenever you think you have been harmed, apply this rule: if the city is not harmed by this, neither am I. But if the city is harmed, you must not be angry with the one who harms it, but show him what he has overlooked.

23. Think often of how fast the things that are, and the things that come to be, are carried past and away. For substance is like a river in constant flow; its activities are in continual change, its causes in countless variations, and hardly anything stands still, not even what is close at hand. And the boundless gulf of the past and of the future, in which all things vanish. How, then, is he not a fool who is puffed up by these things, or torn by them, or complains as if they had troubled him for some time, and for long?
24. Remember the whole of substance, of which you have a tiny share; and the whole of time, of which a short and momentary span has been marked out for you; and fate: how small a part of it are you?

25. Someone does me wrong? That is his business. He has his own disposition, his own activity. I have now what the common nature wants me to have now, and I am doing what my own nature wants me to do now.

26. Let the ruling and governing part of your soul stay unmoved by the smooth or rough movements of the flesh; let it not mix with them, but mark itself off, and keep those feelings within their own parts. And when they rise up into the mind through that other sympathy, as they must in a body that is all one, then you must not try to resist the sensation, which is natural; but let the ruling mind not add, of itself, the judgement that it is good or bad.

27. “Live with the gods.” And he lives with the gods who constantly shows them that his soul is content with what is given it, and does what is wanted by the spirit that Zeus has given to each of us as guardian and guide, a fragment of himself. And this is each person’s mind and reason.

28. Are you angry with the man whose armpits smell? Are you angry with the man whose breath smells? What good will it do you? He has such a mouth, he has such armpits; such a smell is bound to come from such things. “But the man has reason,” he says, “and could, if he paid attention, understand what is offensive.” Good for you! So you have reason too. Stir up his reasonable disposition with your reasonable disposition; show him, remind him. If he listens, you will cure him, and there is no need for anger.
Neither an actor nor a whore.

29. As you mean to live when you have left this life, so you can live here. But if they do not let you, then leave life, but as one who suffers no harm. “The house is smoky, and I leave it.” Why do you think it a great matter? But as long as nothing of the kind drives me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want; and I want what is in keeping with the nature of a rational and social being.

30. The mind of the whole is social. At any rate, it has made the lower things for the sake of the higher, and fitted the higher ones to one another. You see how it has subordinated, co-ordinated, and given to each its due share, and brought the best together into agreement with one another.

31. How have you behaved up to now towards the gods, your parents, your brother, your wife, your children, your teachers, your tutors, your friends, your relations, your servants? Has your rule towards all of them up to now been, “never to do or say anything wrong to anyone”? And remember what you have been through, and what you have had the strength to bear; and that the story of your life is now complete, and your service finished; and how many beautiful things you have seen, how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have let pass, how many unkind people you have been kind to.

32. Why do unskilled and ignorant souls confound the one who is skilled and knowing? What, then, is the soul that is skilled and knowing? The one that knows the beginning and the end, and the reason that runs through all substance and governs the whole through all time in set cycles.

33. Very soon, ashes or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; and a name is a noise and an echo. And the things so highly valued in life are empty, rotten, small: puppies snapping at each other, quarrelsome children laughing and then at once crying. But good faith and modesty and justice and truth have fled “to Olympus from the wide-wayed earth”. What, then, still keeps you here, if the things of the senses are changeable and never stand still, and the senses are dim and easily deceived, and the poor soul itself is a vapour rising from blood, and to be well thought of by such people is empty? What then? You wait calmly for your end, whether it is being put out or moved elsewhere. And until that time comes, what is enough? What else but to honour and praise the gods, and to do good to people, and to put up with them and keep away from them; and to remember that everything outside the limits of your bit of flesh and breath is neither yours nor up to you.

34. You can always have a life that flows smoothly, if you can go by the right road, and think and act by the right road. These two things are common to the soul of God, and of man, and of every rational being: not to be hindered by anything else; and to find the good in a just disposition and just action, and there to let desire come to an end.
35. If this is neither a vice of mine, nor an act that comes from a vice of mine, and the common good is not harmed, why am I troubled about it? And what is the harm to the common good?

36. Do not be swept away entirely by the impression, but help people as far as you can and as they deserve, even if their loss is in indifferent things. But do not imagine it to be a harm; that is a bad habit. Be like the old man who, as he went away, asked back his foster-child’s spinning top, remembering that it was only a top. So too here. Since you are standing on the platform, making speeches: “Man, have you forgotten what these things were?” “Yes; but they matter very much to these people.” “Is that a reason for you to be a fool too?”
“Once, wherever I was caught, I was a fortunate man.” But to be fortunate is to have given yourself a good fortune; and good fortunes are good turns of the soul, good impulses, good actions.
## Book Six

1. The substance of the whole is obedient and easily shaped; and the reason that governs it has no cause in itself for doing harm. For it has no badness, nor does it do anything badly, nor is anything harmed by it. Everything comes into being and is completed according to it.

2. Let it make no difference to you whether you are cold or warm when you do what is right, whether sleepy or well rested, whether spoken badly of or praised, whether dying or doing something else. For dying too is one of the acts of life; so here too it is enough to do the present thing well.
3. Look within. Do not let the special quality or the value of anything slip past you.
4. All the things that exist will very soon change: they will either be turned to vapour, if all substance is one, or be scattered.
5. The reason that governs knows its own state, and what it is doing, and on what material.
6. The best way to take revenge is not to become like the wrongdoer.
7. Take delight and rest in one thing: passing from one act for the common good to another act for the common good, with God in mind.
8. The ruling mind is what wakes itself and turns itself, and makes itself whatever it wants to be, and makes everything that happens appear to itself as it wants it to.
